title: Hospital-Physician Integration and the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement Program

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Hospital-Physician Integration and the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement Program》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · section1-10775587261468837-p5】In our study, we exploited this natural experiment by examining the relationship between the CJR program and the treatment pathway of patients with hip or knee osteoarthritis and, critically, assessed whether this relationship varied across competing organizational models (vertically integrated vs. not vertically integrated). Our first objective was to assess whether CJR influenced the osteoarthritis treatment path. The CJR program imposed financial risks on hospitals performing joint replacements. We believed hospitals would be cautious about assuming financial risk for procedures that were previously reimbursed on a fee-for-service basis, so we expected that they might respond to CJR by actually reducing their volume of joint replacement procedures. Second, we sought to assess whether the hospital integration status of the physician directing a patient’s care independently influenced the osteoarthritis treatment path. Because physician discretion influences many decisions along the treatment path, we expected that hospital-integrated orthopedists, ceteris paribus, would direct their patients toward less conservative treatment, that is, away from visits with physicians and toward total joint replacements. Our rationale was that orthopedists managing this care have substantial influence over the patient’s treatment path and that the hospitals employing orthopedists will lean toward more intensive, hospital-based treatments compared with conservative treatments or wait-and-see approaches. We also sought to test whether there was an interaction between CJR and integration. Our reasoning: CJR imposes risks on providers for costly or poorly coordinated care, but this risk is likely smaller among integrated hospital-physician systems. Many have speculated that hospitals and physicians have integrated for exactly this reason – that is, to better coordinate care and respond to alternative payment models (Post et al., 2018). We therefore expect patients of integrated orthopedists to exhibit less CJR avoidance compared with their non-integrated counterparts.

【Introduction · section1-10775587261468837-p6】Finally, we sought to test whether CJR affected surgical setting (inpatient vs. outpatient). For certain windows during our study period, outpatient surgeries were exempt from the CJR program. We expected CJR hospitals to shift care to the outpatient setting to avoid the risks of the CJR program.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Hospital-Physician Integration and the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement Program》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Introduction · section1-10775587261468837-p1】Hip and knee replacements are by far the most popular elective surgeries among older adults. Over half a million are performed annually on Medicare patients, with even greater use projected over the next decade (Shichman et al., 2023). At the same time, orthopedic care, much like other specialties, has become more closely integrated with hospitals; more orthopedic surgeons (hereafter, orthopedists) than at any other time in history are hospital employees rather than independent practitioners (Machta et al., 2020). However, orthopedic care has been comparatively overlooked in recent studies of hospital–physician integration.

【Introduction · section1-10775587261468837-p2】Despite growing literature over the last decade that hospital–physician integration generally results in higher health care costs with questionable value to patients, two prominent gaps in our understanding remain (Harris et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2019; Richards et al., 2022; Whaley et al., 2021; Young et al., 2021). First, in the context of integration, orthopedic care is one of the comparatively less studied specialties. This is curious for several reasons, above all because orthopedic care is well known to be a lucrative, high-volume service line for hospitals – one that cross-subsidizes service lines like psychiatry that cut into hospitals’ profit margins (David et al., 2014). Employment of orthopedists may therefore be of special strategic importance to hospitals as they seek to secure orthopedic referrals.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Hospital-Physician Integration and the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement Program》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · section14-10775587261468837-p1】Our study demonstrates that when it comes to managing one of the most common orthopedic conditions among Medicare patients, payment paradigm and vertical integration both shape treatment decisions, but in opposite directions – and, in this case, with payment paradigm apparently the stronger force. Policymakers seeking to reduce costs may find bundled payment to be an effective lever even when applied to organizational arrangements that incentivize higher-intensity care.

【Introduction · section1-10775587261468837-p3】At the same time, physician behavior has been shown to be malleable; a physician’s organization, peer group, and financial incentives influence treatment style, particularly when there is latitude for clinical discretion (Post et al., 2023; Reschovsky et al., 2015; Young et al., 2023). Orthopedists in fee-for-service already face incentives to perform surgeries, as procedures tend to generate more revenue than conservative care. Hospital–physician integration, however, may amplify those incentives further. In a typical knee replacement episode, for example, the Medicare physician fee for the surgeon is about $1,200, but the payment to the hospital is about $13,000 (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). Since hospitals gain facility fees and downstream post-acute referrals from surgical episodes, they may encourage their employed orthopedists to prioritize surgical options. A countervailing force is that employed physicians are typically salaried, which may reduce physician effort, as has been found among some physicians after hospital integration (Post et al., 2023). Whether integration increases or decreases surgical utilization remains an open empirical question.

Policymakers seeking to reduce costs may find bundled payment to be an effective lever even when applied to organizational arrangements that incentivize higher-intensity care.

At the same time, physician behavior has been shown to be malleable; a physician’s organization, peer group, and financial incentives influence treatment style, particularly when there is latitude for clinical discretion (Post et al., 2023; Reschovsky et al., 2015; Young et al., 2023). In a typical knee replacement episode, for example, the Medicare physician fee for the surgeon is about $1,200, but the payment to the hospital is about $13,000 (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). Since hospitals gain facility fees and downstream post-acute referrals from surgical episodes, they may encourage their employed orthopedists to prioritize surgical options. A countervailing force is that employed physicians are typically salaried, which may reduce physician effort, as has been found among some physicians after hospital integration (Post et al., 2023). Whether integration increases or decreases surgical utilization remains an open empirical question.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Hospital-Physician Integration and the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement Program》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Figure 1. · fig1-10775587261468837】Figure 1. Visit counts by CJR and VI status.Note. Predicted counts from negative binomial regressions with CJR × VI × Year interactions, adjusted for joint type and covariates. For PCP visits, the average marginal effect of CJR was 0.139 (p < .001) and the average marginal effect of VI was −0.161 (p < .001). For orthopedist visits, the average marginal effect of CJR was 0.231 (p < .001) and the average marginal effect of VI was −0.590 (p < .001). CJR = Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement; VI = vertically integrated.

【Figure 2. · fig2-10775587261468837】Figure 2. Estimated effects of CJR on joint replacement.Note. Linear probability model of the estimated effects of CJR on the probability of a total knee or hip arthroplasty, adjusted for joint type and covariates. Sample-wide probability of surgery: 13.2%. The average marginal effect of the CJR program was −1.9 percentage points (p < .001). The difference in the effect of the CJR program among patients of vertically integrated and non-vertically integrated orthopedists was not statistically significant (p = .3898). The average marginal effect of vertical integration on surgery probability was 1.0 percentage points (p < .001). CJR = Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement; VI = vertically integrated.

【Figure 3. · fig3-10775587261468837】Figure 3. Effects of CJR on outpatient surgical setting.Note. Linear probability model of the estimated effects of CJR on the probability of receiving surgery in the outpatient rather than inpatient setting, adjusted for covariates. Shading indicates periods when outpatient surgery was permitted but exempt from the CJR bundle. Knee sample: N = 6,627, sample-wide OP rate = 48.1%. Reference quarter: 2017q4 (not plotted). The average marginal effect of CJR was −4.6 percentage points (p < .001). Hip sample: N = 4,828, sample-wide OP rate = 55.5%. Reference quarter: 2019q4 (not plotted). The average marginal effect of CJR was −0.7 percentage points (p = .6072). CJR = Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement; OP = outpatient.
